findings.source_passage: I was within and without, simultaneously enchanted and repelled by the inexhaustible variety of life.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'I wanted to get out and walk eastward'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence is verbatim in the draft, which is correct — noting it here only for completeness. No issue found.

findings.source_passage: The supercilious assumption was that on Sunday afternoon I had nothing better to do.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'I think he'd tanked up a good deal at luncheon'
findings.why_it_matters: This sardonic aside is a definitive example of Nick's ironic, self-aware narrative voice; its complete excision flattens the narrator's consciousness at a key early moment.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence after 'his determination bordered on violence.'

findings.source_passage: a sort of compact Main Street ministering to it, and contiguous to absolutely nothing
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'I followed him over a low whitewashed railroad fence'
findings.why_it_matters: The phrase 'compact Main Street ministering to it' is Fitzgerald's distinctive satirical description of the wasteland's pathetic commercial strip; the draft reduces it to 'contiguous to absolutely nothing' alone, losing the ironic sociological image.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'a sort of compact Main Street ministering to it' before 'contiguous to absolutely nothing.'

findings.source_passage: It had occurred to me that this shadow of a garage must be a blind, and that sumptuous and romantic apartments were concealed overhead
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The interior was unprosperous and bare'
findings.why_it_matters: This sentence reveals Nick's ironic romantic imagination and his sense of the gap between aspiration and reality — a key voice-establishing moment in this chapter that the draft entirely omits.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Nick's aside about suspecting the garage to be a blind concealing 'sumptuous and romantic apartments.'

findings.source_passage: His acquaintances resented the fact that he turned up in popular cafés with her and, leaving her at a table, sauntered about, chatting with whomsoever he knew.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The fact that he had one was insisted upon'
findings.why_it_matters: This detail establishes Tom's brazen, class-inflected social performance with his mistress; the draft jumps directly to the train encounter, erasing interpretive material about Tom's character.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the sentence about Tom's café behavior between 'insisted upon wherever he was known' and the train scene.

findings.source_passage: though I was curious to see her, I had no desire to meet her—but I did.
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'The fact that he had one was insisted upon'
findings.why_it_matters: Nick's admission of curiosity against his better judgment is a characteristic voice register — self-awareness undercut by complicity — and is absent from the draft.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore Nick's admission of curiosity versus desire before describing the train journey.

findings.source_passage: Myrtle's first meeting with Tom — the taxi-subway confusion, 'I was so excited that when I got into a taxi with him I didn't hardly know I wasn't getting into a subway train.'
findings.source_locator: paragraph beginning 'Myrtle pulled her chair close to mine'
findings.why_it_matters: The draft gives only a skeleton of Myrtle's speech (dress suit, patent leather, shirtfront) and jumps to the famous closing line, omitting the telling detail of the taxi/subway confusion that characterises Myrtle's social disorientation and the comedy of her excitement.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the taxi-subway confusion sentence from Myrtle's monologue before the 'You can't live forever' line.

findings.source_passage: the dim enlargement of Mrs. Wilson's mother which hovered like an ectoplasm on the wall
findings.why_it_matters: 'Like an ectoplasm' is a textually distinctive, critically noted simile that contributes to the chapter's atmosphere of ghosts and unreality; the draft mentions the photograph but drops the simile entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'hovered like an ectoplasm on the wall' when describing the McKee photograph.

findings.source_passage: the late afternoon sky bloomed in the window for a moment like the blue honey of the Mediterranean
findings.source_locator: paragraph after the Monte Carlo exchange, before Mrs. McKee's 'little kike' remark
findings.why_it_matters: This one-sentence lyrical intrusion — a signature Fitzgerald prose poem — breaks the vulgar party chatter with a sudden beauty; its absence depletes the chapter's tonal contrast.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the 'blue honey of the Mediterranean' sentence as a standalone beat between the Catherine conversation and Mrs. McKee's speech.

findings.source_passage: "Where?" "Anywhere." "Keep your hands off the lever," snapped the elevator boy. "I beg your pardon," said Mr. McKee with dignity, "I didn't know I was touching it."
findings.why_it_matters: The elevator-boy exchange is a surreal, comic-absurdist coda that contributes to the dreamlike dissolution of the scene; the draft drops the elevator boy's line and McKee's dignity entirely.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the three-line exchange with the elevator boy after 'Anywhere.'

summary: The draft contains multiple high- and medium-severity signature losses including the erasure of Nick's ironic aside about Sunday afternoons, the 'compact Main Street' image, the 'shadow of a garage' romantic aside, the 'ectoplasm' simile, and the flattening of Myrtle's full monologue, collectively constituting both voice erasure and significant interpretive thinning.
